title: CSC3710 2026-09-22 — Regex Identities and Intro to DFAs

questions.q: Which regular expression describes the strings over {a, b} of length exactly 2?
questions.explain: Each of the two positions can hold any symbol, so concatenate two copies of (a ∪ b). (a ∪ b)\*(a ∪ b)\* is every string (it equals (a ∪ b)\* by identity 13); ab ∪ ba misses aa and bb; (ab)\* contains λ, abab, ….

questions.q: Let s = (a ∪ b ∪ c). Which expressions describe the strings over {a, b, c} of length greater than three (i.e. at least four)?
questions.explain: "Greater than three" means at least four symbols. Forcing four symbols and allowing anything after (ssss s\*) or before (s\* ssss) works, and sss s⁺ also forces 3 + at least 1 = 4. sss s\* allows length 3, and ssss s⁺ forces at least 5, so it misses the length-4 strings.

questions.q: Which expressions describe the strings over {a, b} of length two or more in which all a's precede all b's?
questions.explain: The set is aⁱbʲ with i + j ≥ 2. a⁺b⁺ covers the strings with at least one of each; aa⁺ and bb⁺ add the all-a and all-b strings (the condition is vacuously true for them). a\*(aa ∪ ab ∪ bb)b\* works too: every such string has aa, ab or bb at the seam. a\*b\* wrongly includes λ, a and b; a⁺b⁺ and aa\*bb\* (which is the same set) miss aa, bb, aaa, ….

questions.q: A student answers a⁺b⁺ for "strings over {a, b} of length ≥ 2 in which all a's precede all b's". What is wrong with it?
choices: It misses strings made only of a's or only of b's, such as aa and bbb
It includes the single strings a and b
questions.explain: a⁺b⁺ demands at least one a and at least one b. But aa, aaa, bb, bbb, … also satisfy "all a's precede all b's" (vacuously), so they belong. The fix is a⁺b⁺ ∪ aa⁺ ∪ bb⁺.

questions.q: Why is a\*b\* not a correct answer for "length ≥ 2, all a's precede all b's" over {a, b}?
choices: It contains strings shorter than 2, such as λ, a and b
questions.explain: a\*b\* gets the ordering right but ignores the length condition: taking zero or one copies gives λ, a and b. The equivalence checker reports λ as a counterexample.

questions.q: Which expressions describe the strings over {a, b} that contain the substring ab and have length at least 3?
questions.explain: A string of length ≥ 3 containing ab has at least one extra symbol just before or just after some ab. The first answer says exactly that; the second lists the four length-3 cores containing ab. They look different but are the same set (identities 9 and 10 convert one into the other). (a ∪ b)\*ab(a ∪ b)\* includes ab itself (length 2). (a ∪ b)⁺ab(a ∪ b)\* misses aba and abb, where no symbol precedes the ab.

questions.q: Which expression describes the strings over {a, b} that end in ba and have length at least 3?
questions.explain: The string must finish with ba and have at least one symbol before it: one forced symbol, then anything, then ba. Equivalently (a ∪ b)⁺ba. (a ∪ b)\*ba includes ba (length 2); the other two don't end in ba.

questions.q: Which expressions describe the strings over {a, b} of length less than three?
questions.explain: List by length: λ (length 0), a, b (length 1), and (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b) (length 2). The product (λ ∪ a ∪ b)(λ ∪ a ∪ b) gives the same set because each factor may contribute nothing. Dropping λ misses the empty string; (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b) is length exactly 2.

questions.q: How many strings over {a, b} of length at most 2 have every a before every b?
questions.explain: All strings of length ≤ 2: λ, a, b, aa, ab, ba, bb — seven of them. Only ba has an a after a b, so 6 remain: λ ∪ a ∪ b ∪ aa ∪ ab ∪ bb.

questions.q: Every regular set has exactly one regular expression that describes it.
questions.explain: False. Many different regular expressions describe the same set — e.g. the two answers for "contains ab, length ≥ 3". That is exactly why identities and equivalence proofs are needed.

questions.q: A regular expression that uses no Kleene star always describes a finite set.
questions.explain: True. The basic sets are finite, and union and concatenation of finite sets are finite. Only the star can produce infinitely many strings.

questions.q: Any regular expression containing a Kleene star describes an infinite set.
questions.explain: False. ∅\* = λ and λ\* = λ both describe the finite set {λ}. A star makes the set infinite only when it is applied to a set containing a non-empty string.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a valid regular expression over {a, b} in textbook notation?
questions.explain: Regular expressions are built from symbols, λ and ∅ using ∪, concatenation, \* and parentheses — in any combination and depth. A dangling operator like "a ∪" with nothing after it breaks the construction rules. ∅\* is perfectly valid (it equals λ).

questions.q: Choose the regular set(s) over {a, b} to which the string abba belongs.
questions.explain: (a ∪ ab)\*ba: abba = ab · ba, with ab ∈ (a ∪ ab)\*. The others fail by an invariant: in (a ∪ ab)\* every b directly follows an a, so bb never appears; every string in (a ∪ b)\*ab ends in b, but abba ends in a; every string in (aba ∪ bab)(ab ∪ ba) has length 5, but abba has length 4.

questions.q: Why can abba never be in (a ∪ ab)\*?
choices: Every b in such a string comes directly after an a, so bb cannot appear
Every string in the set ends in b
Every string in the set has odd length
questions.explain: The building blocks are a and ab. Gluing them together, each b is always immediately preceded by the a in its own block, so the substring bb never occurs. abba contains bb, so it is excluded.

questions.q: Choose the regular set(s) over {a, b} to which baab belongs.
questions.explain: (a ∪ b)\*aa(a ∪ b)\*: baab = b · aa · b. (ba ∪ ab)\*: baab = ba · ab. b(ab)\*a gives ba, baba, …, never containing aa. In (b ∪ ab)\* every a is immediately followed by b, so aa cannot occur.

questions.q: What is the general technique for showing that a string is NOT in the set described by a regular expression?
choices: Find an invariant — a property every string in the set has that your string lacks
Try a few decompositions and give up if none works
Show the string is longer than the expression
Show the string contains a symbol that appears in the expression
questions.explain: Find a property shared by all members — "ends in b", "never contains bb", "has length exactly 5" — that the string fails. One such observation settles the question with nothing else to check.

questions.q: To show a string IS in the set described by a regular expression, what is enough?
choices: One explicit decomposition of the string that matches the expression
Every possible decomposition of the string
Showing the string has the right length
Listing all strings of the set up to that length
questions.explain: Give one way to cut the string into pieces, each piece from the matching part of the expression (e.g. abba = ab · b · a). Strings can often be built more than one way, but a single construction proves membership.

questions.q: With the online equivalence checker, how can you test whether a string w belongs to L(R)?
choices: Compare R with w|R: they are equivalent exactly when w ∈ L(R)
Compare R with w: they are equivalent exactly when w ∈ L(R)
questions.explain: Adding a string that is already in the set changes nothing (identity 7, u ∪ u = u). So R and w ∪ R describe the same set if and only if w was already in L(R). Comparing R with just w would only be equivalent if R's set were {w}.

questions.q: The tool lists strings of a set in order of length. If it has moved on to length-5 strings and never produced abba, then abba is not in the set.
questions.explain: True. Strings appear shortest first, so every length-4 member would have appeared before any length-5 string. abba has length 4.

questions.q: A multiple-select question has 5 options worth equal shares. A and C are true; B, D, E are false. A student checks A, B and C. Under the course's per-option grading, what percent does the student earn?
questions.explain: Each option is scored separately: A true & checked (earned), B false but checked (lost), C true & checked (earned), D and E false & unchecked (earned). 4 of 5 options = 80 %.

questions.q: For the baab question with options A (a ∪ b)\*aa(a ∪ b)\*, B b(ab)\*a, C (ba ∪ ab)\*, D (b ∪ ab)\*, a student checks A and D only. What percent does per-option grading give?
questions.explain: True options are A and C. A checked & true (+1), B unchecked & false (+1), C missed (0), D checked but false (0): 2/4 = 50 %.

questions.q: In this course, a multiple-select (square checkbox) question may have no correct options at all.
questions.explain: False. At least one option is always correct; "choose none" is never the intended answer.

questions.q: Which string belongs to (b ∪ ab)\*?
questions.explain: babb = b · ab · b. In (b ∪ ab)\* every a must be immediately followed by b, so aa (in baab, aab) is impossible, and abba ends in an a with nothing after it.

questions.q: Which string is NOT in (ab)\*a?
questions.explain: (ab)\*a = {a, aba, ababa, …}: (ab)ⁿ followed by a. Every member ends in a and has odd length; abab ends in b.

questions.q: What is ∅u (and u∅) equal to?
questions.explain: Identity 1. Concatenation needs a prefix from the first set and a suffix from the second; ∅ has no strings to supply, so no strings can be formed.

questions.q: Why is ∅\* = λ?
choices: Because any set to the 0th power is {λ}, and all higher powers of ∅ are ∅
Because ∅ and λ are the same thing
Because star always adds λ to a non-empty set only
questions.explain: Identity 3. ∅\* = ∅⁰ ∪ ∅¹ ∪ ∅² ∪ … = {λ} ∪ ∅ ∪ ∅ ∪ … = {λ}. X⁰ = {λ} for every set X, even ∅.

questions.q: ∅ and {λ} are the same set.
questions.explain: False. ∅ has no elements; {λ} has exactly one element, the empty string. This difference is why ∅u = ∅ but λu = u.

questions.q: Which of these is FALSE in general?
questions.explain: Concatenation distributes over union (identities 9 and 10), but it is not commutative. In u(v ∪ w), u stays glued on the left: uv ∪ uw. Moving u to the right changes the set (e.g. a(b ∪ c) = {ab, ac} ≠ {ba, ca}).

questions.q: Which of these are equal to (u ∪ v)\* for all regular expressions u, v?
questions.explain: All forms of identity 12 mean "any sequence of u-pieces and v-pieces". u\*v\* only allows all u's before all v's (no vu), and (uv)\* forces strict alternation starting with u.

questions.q: Which is identity 11?
questions.explain: Both sides are u, uvu, uvuvu, …: u and v alternate, starting and ending with u. Only the grouping differs, and concatenation is associative. Example: (ab)\*a = a(ba)\* = {a, aba, ababa, …}.

questions.q: Identity 12 form 1 says (u\* ∪ v)\* = (u ∪ v)\*. When may you delete a star this way?
choices: Only when the star sits on one whole operand of a union that is itself entirely under an outer star
Whenever a star appears anywhere inside another star
Whenever the star is on a single symbol
questions.explain: The inner star is redundant only because the outer star already allows any number of u-pieces. In (b\* ∪ b\*ab\*)\* you may remove the star from the standalone b\*, but not the stars inside b\*ab\*, because they don't cover a whole operand of the union.

questions.q: Which identity did the instructor add to the textbook table (identity 13 on the course sheet)?
questions.explain: Two runs of u-pieces in a row are one run of u-pieces, so u\*u\* = u\*. It was used in the worked proof to turn b\*b\* into b\*. The others are false in general (u\*u and uu\* are u⁺, which lacks λ unless λ ∈ u; u\* ∪ v\* misses mixed strings).

questions.q: What set fact is behind identity 7, u ∪ u = u?
choices: Repeated elements don't matter in a set
Adding the empty set changes nothing
questions.explain: A set either contains an element or not; listing it twice changes nothing (e.g. ℕ ∪ ℕ = ℕ). Commutativity is identity 5 and u ∪ ∅ = u is identity 6.

questions.q: Why is (u\*)\* = u\* (identity 8)?
choices: Any concatenation of strings from u\* is itself a concatenation of u-pieces, so nothing new appears
Because the outer star removes λ
questions.explain: Using the whole set u\* as building blocks never creates a new string: each block (e.g. aa) is already built from u-pieces, so gluing blocks just gives longer runs of u-pieces, all already in u\*.

questions.q: Which of these always hold?
questions.explain: u⁺ is one or more copies, so it equals uu\* = u\*u, and adding λ gives u\*. λ ∈ u⁺ only if λ ∈ u. (u\*)⁺ = u\* because u\* already contains λ and is closed under concatenation.

questions.q: (ab ∪ λ)b\* = abb\* ∪ λb\* uses which identity and substitution?
choices: 10: (u ∪ v)w = uw ∪ vw, with u = ab, v = λ, w = b\*
9: u(v ∪ w) = uv ∪ uw, with u = b\*, v = ab, w = λ
12 form 1, with u = b, v = ab
questions.explain: The union is on the left and b\* is appended on the right, so it is right distribution (identity 10) with w = b\*.

questions.q: (b\* ∪ ab)\* = (b ∪ ab)\* uses which identity?
choices: 12 form 1: (u\* ∪ v)\* = (u ∪ v)\*, with u = b, v = ab
11: (uv)\*u = u(vu)\*, with u = a, v = b
questions.explain: A starred operand (b\*) of a union that is entirely under a star loses its inner star: form 1 with u = b and v = ab.

questions.q: (ab)\*a = a(ba)\* uses which identity?
choices: 12 form 6 with u = a, v = b
questions.explain: This is (uv)\*u = u(vu)\* with u = a and v = b.

questions.q: a\*a\*b = a\*b uses which identity?
choices: 7: u ∪ u = u, with u = a\*
questions.explain: The prefix a\*a\* collapses to a\* by the course's added identity 13; the b is simply concatenated afterward.

questions.q: Before trying to prove two regular expressions equal with identities, what should you do first?
choices: Check with the equivalence tool / look for a counterexample string
Convert both to DFAs by hand
Count the stars on each side
questions.explain: If they are not equal, a single counterexample string (in one set but not the other) proves it, and no proof exists. The tool finds such a string automatically; if it says "Equivalent", a proof exists.

questions.q: In proving (a ∪ b)\* = (b\*(a ∪ λ)b\*)\*, the first step rewrites (b\*(a ∪ λ)b\*)\* as ((b\*a ∪ b\*λ)b\*)\*. Which identity and substitution is that?
choices: 9 with u = b\*, v = a, w = λ
10 with u = a, v = λ, w = b\*
12 form 1 with u = b, v = a
questions.explain: The b\* on the left is distributed into the union (a ∪ λ): u(v ∪ w) = uv ∪ uw with u = b\*, v = a, w = λ. The trailing b\* is handled next by identity 10.

questions.q: The step (b\*ab\* ∪ b\*b\*)\* → (b\*ab\* ∪ b\*)\* uses which identity?
questions.explain: b\*b\* is two runs of b's, which is one run of b's: the instructor-added identity 13.

questions.q: In the step (b\* ∪ b\*ab\*)\* → (b ∪ b\*ab\*)\*, identity 12 form 1 is applied. What are u and v?
questions.explain: The key idea is to treat the whole of b\*ab\* as a single expression v. Then (b\* ∪ b\*ab\*)\* has the shape (u\* ∪ v)\* with u = b, and the inner star on b\* can be deleted.

questions.q: The step (b ∪ b\*ab\*)\* → (b ∪ b\*a)\* uses identity 12 form 3, (u ∪ vu\*)\* = (u ∪ v)\*. What substitution makes it work?
choices: u = b, v = b\*a, so vu\* = b\*ab\*
questions.explain: b\*ab\* has the shape vu\* with v = b\*a and u = b. Then (u ∪ vu\*)\* collapses to (u ∪ v)\* = (b ∪ b\*a)\*. Choosing the right split is the hard part of these proofs.

questions.q: Which chain proves (a\* ∪ ba\*)\* = (a ∪ b)\*?
choices: 12 form 1 (u = a, v = ba\*) gives (a ∪ ba\*)\*, then 12 form 3 (u = a, v = b) gives (a ∪ b)\*
questions.explain: First delete the star on the standalone a\* (form 1), giving (a ∪ ba\*)\*. That has the shape (u ∪ vu\*)\* with u = a, v = b, which form 3 collapses to (a ∪ b)\*.

questions.q: To prove (a ∪ b)\*b\* = (a ∪ b)\*, you can rewrite (b ∪ a)\*b\* as (b\*a)\*b\*b\* and then simplify. Which identity performs the rewriting (b ∪ a)\* = (b\*a)\*b\*?
choices: 12 form 6: (u ∪ v)\* = (u\*v)\*u\*, with u = b, v = a
questions.explain: Form 6 turns (b ∪ a)\* into (b\*a)\*b\*, so the trailing b\* joins it to make b\*b\*, which identity 13 reduces to b\*. Reading form 6 backwards then returns (b ∪ a)\*, and identity 5 swaps to (a ∪ b)\*.

questions.q: Transforming both sides of an equation in parallel until they reach a common expression is a valid identity proof.
questions.explain: True. Equality is transitive: if L = E and R = E, then L = R. You may also start from either side; starting from the more complicated side is usually easier.

questions.q: Long identity-chain proofs like (a ∪ b)\* = (b\*(a ∪ λ)b\*)\* will appear on tests.
questions.explain: False. The instructor said a proof that long could take the whole test. They are practice only (5 more exercises with an answer key); any review question of this kind will be easy.

questions.q: A shorter set-based proof of (a ∪ b)\* ⊆ (b\*(a ∪ λ)b\*)\* observes that the right side R contains a and b. Why does that suffice?
choices: R is starred, so it contains every concatenation of its members — hence every string of a's and b's
Because a and b are the only symbols, R must equal {a, b}
questions.explain: a = λ·a·λ and b = b·λ·λ are in the starred body, and a star is closed under concatenation, so every string over {a, b} is in R. The reverse inclusion is trivial since R only uses a's and b's. If a question says "use the identities", though, you must give the identity chain.

questions.q: What must you state at each step of an identity proof?
choices: Which identity is used and what u, v (and w) stand for
The number of strings added at that step
questions.explain: Name the identity and give the substitution. A "perfect proof" even writes small steps like b\*λb\* → b\*b\* (identity 2) as their own line.

questions.q: In the online equivalence checker, how do you write a ∪ λ?
questions.explain: The tool has no λ key. λ is an empty alternative, so a ∪ λ becomes `(a|)` — "ugly, but it works" — or the optional operator `a?`. `!` is JFLAP's notation, not the checker's.

questions.q: When two expressions are not equivalent, what does the checker report?
choices: A counterexample: a shortest string accepted by one but not the other
The number of strings that differ
questions.explain: It prints a single string "accepted by first but not second" (or vice versa). That one string is itself a complete proof that the expressions differ.

questions.q: JFLAP exports the expression (a+b)\*ab. What should you paste into the equivalence checker?
questions.explain: JFLAP writes union as +, but in the checker + means "one or more". Replace every + with | before pasting, or the comparison will be wrong.

questions.q: JFLAP shows the empty string as λ (typed `!`). How must (a+!) be written for the checker?
questions.explain: Replace + with | and the empty string with an empty alternative: `(a|)`.

questions.q: You designed a DFA in JFLAP for a given regular expression. How do you check it?
choices: Convert → Convert FA to RE, export the expression, and compare it with the given one in the equivalence checker
Run one string through the DFA
Count the states and compare with the number of stars
Convert the given expression to a table by hand
questions.explain: JFLAP converts the machine to an equivalent regular expression; if the checker says it is equivalent to the target, the DFA is correct, and otherwise the counterexample shows where it goes wrong.

questions.q: The online regular-expression tool may be used during tests and reviews.
questions.explain: True — the instructor stressed you will always be able to use it. The link is in the syllabus and on Teams.

questions.q: In the checker, what does `(a|b)^3` describe?
choices: All strings over {a, b} of length exactly 3
All strings of length at most 3
The string (a|b) repeated with a star
Strings with three a's or three b's
questions.explain: `^N` means exactly N copies, so `(a|b)^3` = (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)(a ∪ b).

questions.q: How can the checker list the strings of an expression R, shortest first?
choices: Put R in the first box, leave the second empty, then keep adding each reported string to the second box
Put R\* in the first box
questions.explain: An empty box means {λ}, so the tool reports the shortest string of R not in the second box. Adding it (e.g. `aa`, then `aa|aaa`) makes the tool show the next one — a good way to test whether your expression grabs exactly the right strings.

questions.q: Which is the formal definition of a DFA?
questions.explain: Five components: a finite set of states Q, an alphabet Σ, a transition function δ, an initial state q₀, and a set of final states F. All five must be specified.

questions.q: Which of the following are requirements of the DFA definition?
choices: δ : Q × Σ → Q is a total function
There is exactly one final state
questions.explain: The only constraint on F is F ⊆ Q, so F may be empty or have many states. Q must be finite, there is exactly one initial state in Q, and δ must be total.

questions.q: A DFA may have no final states (F = ∅).
questions.explain: True. ∅ is a subset of every set, so F = ∅ satisfies F ⊆ Q. "Weird, but we accept it" — like the empty language.

questions.q: Every state of a DFA may be final (F = Q).
questions.explain: True. Q ⊆ Q, so F = Q is allowed.

questions.q: What language does a DFA accept if F = ∅, and if F = Q?
choices: F = ∅: the empty language ∅; F = Q: Σ\*
questions.explain: With F = ∅, no computation ends in a final state, so nothing is accepted. With F = Q, every computation ends in a final state, so every string is accepted. Note ∅ ≠ {λ}.

questions.q: The game-book "monster attitude" state machine had 5 states and 5 inputs, no initial-state arrow, no final states, and some missing arrows. Which features keep it from being a DFA?
questions.explain: A DFA needs exactly one initial state and a total δ (5 × 5 = 25 arrows here). Having no final states is allowed.

questions.q: In the rest of this course, what does a final state mean?
choices: The machine accepts the input string if it ends there
Something happens, like releasing a bottle
The machine resets to the initial state
questions.explain: From now on machines are language acceptors: final states mark acceptance. In the vending machine "final" meant an action; machines that do something return only with Turing machines at the end of the course.

questions.q: A DFA may have two initial states.
questions.explain: False. q₀ is a single state with q₀ ∈ Q; exactly one state is the initial state, drawn with an incoming arrow tip.

questions.q: In δ : Q × Σ → Q, what does × denote?
choices: The Cartesian product: all pairs (state, symbol)
Multiplication of the number of states by symbols
questions.explain: The domain of δ is the set of ordered pairs (q, x) with q ∈ Q and x ∈ Σ. δ maps each pair to the next state, like a function delta(state, symbol) → state.

questions.q: A DFA has 4 states and alphabet {0, 1, 2}. How many transitions must it have?
questions.explain: δ has exactly one value for each pair in Q × Σ, so there are |Q| · |Σ| = 4 · 3 = 12 transitions.

questions.q: A DFA has 100 states over the alphabet {a, b}. How many arrows does its state diagram have (counting each (state, symbol) transition once)?
questions.explain: |Q| · |Σ| = 100 · 2 = 200. Every state needs one a-arrow and one b-arrow.

questions.q: How many transitions does the vending-machine DFA (5 states, inputs quarter and half dollar) have?
questions.explain: 5 · 2 = 10 — which is also why writing δ as separate equations would take 10 lines, and a table is neater.

questions.q: A DFA has 7 states and alphabet {a, b, c, d}. How many transitions does it have?
questions.explain: 7 · 4 = 28, one per (state, symbol) pair.

questions.q: A machine over {a, b} has states q₀ (initial) and q₁ (final) with arrows q₀ –a→ q₁, q₀ –b→ q₀, q₁ –a→ q₁, q₁ –b→ q₀, q₁ –b→ q₁. Is it a DFA?
choices: No: δ(q₁, b) would have two values, so δ is not a function
No: q₁ cannot be both final and have a self-loop
questions.explain: Every pair has at least one arrow, so nothing is missing, but q₁ has two b-arrows. A function gives exactly one value per input, so this is not a DFA.

questions.q: If some state has no arrow for some symbol, which part of the DFA definition fails?
choices: δ is not total: it is undefined for that (state, symbol) pair
questions.explain: A (total) function must assign a value to every element of its domain Q × Σ. A missing arrow leaves a pair without a value.

questions.q: A DFA can get stuck on some input string with no arrow to follow.
questions.explain: False. Because δ is total, for every state and every symbol there is exactly one arrow to follow (possibly a self-loop). The vending machine keeps working however many coins you insert.

questions.q: What makes f : A → B a (total) function?
choices: Every element of A is assigned exactly one element of B
Every element of B is hit by some element of A
Some elements of A are assigned an element of B
Each element of B is hit at most once
questions.explain: Total function = exactly one output for every input in the domain. Missing values or two different values both break it. (Hitting all of B would be "onto"; at most once would be "one-to-one" — neither is required.)

questions.q: In the vending machine, what is δ($0.25, half dollar)?
questions.explain: A half dollar adds $0.50 to the $0.25 already inserted: $0.75.

questions.q: In the vending machine, where does a quarter lead from $0.75?
questions.explain: $0.75 + $0.25 = $1. From $0.75 either coin reaches "$1 or more", because the machine gives no change.

questions.q: From the "$1 or more" state, where does a quarter lead?
questions.explain: After releasing a bottle the count restarts from zero, so the machine behaves as if at $0: a quarter goes to $0.25 and a half dollar to $0.50. It does not go back through the $0.00 state.

questions.q: Why is making "$0.00 deposited" the final state (instead of a separate "$1 or more" state) a bad design?
choices: Final means "release a bottle", so the machine would give a bottle as soon as it's plugged in — and again on every replug
The definition forbids the initial state from being final
questions.explain: In this model a final state triggers the bottle. A final initial state means a free bottle on power-up. The definition allows it; it's a modelling choice, and this choice is a bad one.

questions.q: Trace the vending machine on quarter, half dollar, quarter, half dollar, half dollar. How many bottles are released and where does it end?
questions.explain: $0 →q $0.25 →h $0.75 →q $1+ (bottle 1) →h $0.50 →h $1+ (bottle 2). As an acceptor, this input is accepted since it ends in a final state.

questions.q: Run the vending machine as an acceptor on half, quarter, half, quarter. What happens?
choices: It ends in $0.25 and the string is rejected, even though it passed through the final state
It is accepted because it passed through the final state
It ends in $1 or more and is accepted
questions.explain: $0 →h $0.50 →q $0.75 →h $1+ →q $0.25. One bottle came out along the way, but as an acceptor only the state at the end of the input counts: $0.25 ∉ F.

questions.q: In a transition table for δ, what are the rows, columns and entries?
choices: Rows = states, columns = alphabet symbols, entries = next states
Rows = symbols, columns = strings, entries = accept/reject
Rows = states, columns = states, entries = symbols only
questions.explain: Entry (row q, column x) is δ(q, x). The initial state is marked → and final states \* (or circled). It holds the same information as the diagram.

questions.q: On a test you may give a DFA either as a state diagram or as a 5-tuple with a transition table.
questions.explain: True. Both contain exactly the same information. (The instructor joked "if you hate me, go with the table".)

questions.q: A DFA over {a, b} has states q₀ (initial) and q₁ (final); δ(q₀, a) = q₁, δ(q₀, b) = q₀, δ(q₁, a) = q₁, δ(q₁, b) = q₀. Which strings does it accept?
choices: Strings with an odd number of a's
questions.explain: An a always leads to q₁ and a b always leads to q₀, so the current state just records the last symbol read. The machine ends in q₁ exactly when the last symbol is a.

questions.q: How are the initial and final states marked?
choices: Initial: an incoming arrow tip (→ in a table); final: double circle (\* in a table)
Initial: double circle; final: arrow tip
Both are marked with a star
questions.explain: In JFLAP and on paper the initial state has an arrow pointing into it and final states are double circles; in tables use → and \*.

questions.q: The extended transition function δ̂ : Q × Σ\* → Q satisfies δ̂(q, λ) = ?
questions.explain: Reading nothing does not move the machine. The recursive step is δ̂(q, wa) = δ(δ̂(q, w), a).

questions.q: When does a DFA M accept a string w?
choices: When the computation passes through any final state
When w contains a symbol of every final state
questions.explain: Start in q₀, read w left to right following arrows, and accept iff the state reached after the whole string is in F. L(M) = { w ∈ Σ\* | M accepts w }.

questions.q: Because δ is total, δ̂(q₀, w) is defined for every string w ∈ Σ\*.
questions.explain: True. Each symbol always has exactly one arrow to follow, so any string can be read to the end — the formal meaning of "a DFA never gets stuck".

questions.q: In the DFA with δ(q₀, a) = q₁, δ(q₀, b) = q₀, δ(q₁, a) = q₁, δ(q₁, b) = q₀, F = {q₁}, what happens on input abab?
questions.explain: q₀ →a q₁ →b q₀ →a q₁ →b q₀. The final state q₀ ∉ F, so abab is rejected (it doesn't end in a).
